question.prompt:
Consider a decreasing sequence of \(n\) positive integers \(x_1 \gt x_2 \gt x_3 \gt \cdots \gt x_n\) that satisfies the following conditions. The average of the first \(3\) terms in the sequence is \(2025.\) For all \(4 \le k \le n,\) the average of the first \(k\) terms in the sequence is \(1\) less than the average of the first \(k - 1\) terms in the sequence.

What is the greatest possible value of \(n?\)

solutions.title: Subtract consecutive totals
solutions.explanation:
The prescribed averages determine the totals of the first several terms. Subtracting consecutive totals will then determine each later term.

For \(k\ge3\), there have been \(k-3\) decreases in the average, so the average of the first \(k\) terms is
\[
2025-(k-3)=2028-k.
\]
Let \(S_k=x_1+\cdots+x_k\). Multiplying the average by the number of terms gives
\[
S_k=k(2028-k).
\]
For \(k\ge4\), subtracting the total of the first \(k-1\) terms leaves just \(x_k\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_k&=S_k-S_{k-1}\\
&=k(2028-k)-(k-1)(2029-k)\\
&=2029-2k.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(x_4=2021\), and each subsequent term is two smaller. Positivity requires
\[
2029-2k>0,
\qquad k<1014.5.
\]
Since indices are integers, the sequence cannot continue beyond \(k=1014\).

To attain this bound, choose the first three terms to be \(2026,2025,2024\), followed by
\[
2021,2019,2017,\ldots,1.
\]
The first three terms average \(2025\), and the entire sequence is strictly decreasing and positive. Each later term is exactly the difference \(S_k-S_{k-1}\) calculated above, so the constructed sequence has all the prescribed totals and averages. Its last term is \(x_{1014}=1\).

Therefore the greatest possible length is \(\boxed{1014}\), choice \(\mathrm{B}\).

solutions.title: Balance each drop in average
solutions.explanation:
Lowering an average by one imposes a precise deficit on the newly added term. Following that deficit reveals a simple pattern in the later terms.

Suppose the first \(k\) terms average \(A\). Relative to the desired new average \(A-1\), those existing terms have a total surplus of \(k\). To make the average of all \(k+1\) terms equal \(A-1\), the new term must be \(k\) below that new average. Its value must therefore be
\[
x_{k+1}=(A-1)-k=A-(k+1).
\]
At the next step, the old average is one smaller, and the quantity subtracted is one larger. Consequently, the next new term is two smaller.

Starting from three terms averaging \(2025\), the fourth term must be
\[
x_4=2025-4=2021.
\]
All later terms are therefore forced to be
\[
2021,2019,2017,\ldots.
\]
The positive terms in this tail end at \(1\). There are
\[
\frac{2021-1}{2}+1=1011
\]
of them: there are \(1010\) steps of size two between the endpoints, and one more term than steps. The next term would be \(-1\), so no longer positive tail is possible.

This length is attainable. Begin with \(2026,2025,2024\), which average \(2025\), and append the forced tail through \(1\). The sequence is strictly decreasing and positive. The balancing rule shows that each appended term lowers the current average by exactly one.

Including the initial three terms gives
\[
n=3+1011=\boxed{1014},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{B}\).
